title: Mixed Signals: Why Someone Is Hot and Cold, What to Do — cv.cm
description: Mixed signals explained: why someone is hot and cold, a table of patterns and likely reasons, words to ask for clarity, and when to walk away.
h1: What do mixed signals mean, and what should you do?
answer: Mixed signals usually mean the person is unsure, avoids closeness, is busy, is less interested than you, or is keeping options open. You cannot read which from one message. Watch what they do over a few weeks, ask one calm question about where things are going, and decide based on actions, not hopeful words.

body: Mixed signals are when someone's words and actions point in different directions, or when they are warm one week and distant the next. They say "I miss you" but never make a plan. They text every night for a week, then go quiet for five days. They flirt in person and act like a stranger in front of friends.

It feels confusing because your brain wants a clear answer, and the warm moments keep you hoping. Rewards that come at random times are known to keep people checking and waiting more than steady ones. That is why a hot and cold person can take up so much of your attention, even when the relationship gives you little.

Mixed signals are not always a game. Often the other person is confused too. But whether they mean it or not, the effect on you is the same: you spend energy guessing. The aim of this page is to help you stop guessing.

sections.h: Why people are hot and cold
body: There are a handful of common reasons. More than one can be true at once.

ul: They are unsure. They like you but do not know if they want a relationship, or with you.

They avoid closeness. People with a more avoidant attachment style often pull back when things get close, then reach out again when there is some distance. Gottman Institute writers describe how this can meet an anxious partner's need for reassurance and create a cycle that never settles.
They are busy or overloaded. Work, exams, family or health can make contact uneven. This is usually explained and short-lived.
They are less interested than you. They enjoy the attention but do not want more.
They are keeping options open. They are talking to several people and you are one of them.
They are breadcrumbing. They give just enough attention to keep you interested, without planning to commit.

body: Research on first attraction also offers a useful hint: interest that is warm toward everyone tends to mean less than interest aimed at one person. Someone who flirts with the whole room is not sending you a special signal.

body: A single row means little. If most of what you see lives in the middle column under "less interested" or "options", believe the pattern.

sections.h: A simple rule: actions over time
body: Words are easy. Effort is harder. When words and actions disagree, the actions are usually more honest. Look at the last four to six weeks, not the last message.

ol: Count who starts contact. If it is almost always you, that is a signal.
Count plans made and plans kept. Plans that happen show interest. Plans that stay "sometime" do not.
Notice how you feel most days. Calm and looked after, or anxious and checking your phone?
Notice whether things are moving. Closer over time, or stuck in the same place?

body: If the answers point one way, you have your answer, even if the person has not said it.
One calm, honest question is better than months of guessing. Pick a quiet time, ideally in person or on a call, not in the middle of an argument.

ul: "I like spending time with you. Where do you see this going?"
"Sometimes you feel very close, and then I don't hear from you for days. I'd like to understand what's going on for you."
"I'm looking for something steady. Is that something you want too?"
"I don't need an answer tonight, but I'd like to know where we stand soon."

body: Then listen. A clear answer, either way, is good news because it ends the guessing. Watch out for answers that sound nice but change nothing, like "Let's not put labels on it" followed by the same pattern. If you hear that, read what guys mean when they say "Let's see where it goes", and see cv.cm's slang dictionary for what situationship means.
Avoid tests and games: ignoring them to see if they chase, making them jealous, or pretending you do not care. They add more mixed signals from your side and make an honest answer less likely.
It is time to step back if:

ul: You asked clearly and nothing changed after a few weeks.
You feel anxious more often than happy.
You only hear from them when they are bored, lonely or late at night.
They get angry, mock you or punish you with silence when you ask where things stand.
They keep you hidden from friends with no good reason.

body: Stepping back can be simple and kind: "I've enjoyed our time, but I need something more consistent. I'm going to step back. I wish you well." You do not need their agreement. If the pattern is low-effort messages that keep you waiting, read the article on breadcrumbing. cv.cm's attachment style test can also help you see whether your own pattern makes hot and cold people feel extra hard to let go.

body.note: Being confused for a while is normal when you are getting to know someone. Being confused for months, after you have asked, is information.

faq.q: Are mixed signals a sign of attraction?
faq.a: Sometimes. A person can be attracted to you and still be unsure, scared or busy. But attraction without effort is not enough to build on, so judge by what they do over time.

faq.q: Why does someone pull away after getting close?
faq.a: Common reasons are fear of closeness, being unsure about the relationship, or stress elsewhere. A calm question about what happened is more useful than guessing or chasing.

faq.q: Should I ignore someone who gives mixed signals?
faq.a: Ignoring them as a game usually makes things worse. It is better to ask one clear question and then match their effort, or step back honestly if nothing changes.

faq.q: Do people give mixed signals on purpose?
faq.a: Some do, to keep attention without commitment. Many do not mean to and are unsure themselves. Either way, you can decide based on how the pattern affects you.

faq.q: How long should I wait for someone to make up their mind?
faq.a: There is no rule, but a few weeks after a clear conversation is usually enough to see whether anything changes. Waiting months while you feel anxious is a high cost.
